name: Tempranillo

lines.s10: Tempranillo is the heart of Rioja and Ribera del Duero: dried cherry, strawberry and leather, often wrapped in the vanilla of long cask age.
lines.s20: Tempranillo is Spain's signature red, the backbone of Rioja and, as Tinto Fino, of Ribera del Duero. It gives strawberry, dried cherry and leather at medium weight, and years in American oak add vanilla and coconut.
lines.s45: Tempranillo is Spain's own red, the grape of Rioja on the upper Ebro and, as Tinto Fino, of Ribera del Duero on the high plateau. It tastes of strawberry, red plum and dried cherry, with leather and tobacco, at medium weight with a fresh, fine grip. The cellar does the rest. Traditional Rioja spends years in American oak barrels, which add vanilla, coconut and dill, and the label says how long: Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva. Ribera is darker and firmer, more often in French oak. Pour it with roast lamb, chorizo or Manchego. Temprano means early, and the grape earns the name, ripening weeks before most of Spain's other reds.
lines.sale: Tempranillo has done its waiting for you: a Rioja Reserva ages at least three years, part in barrel and part in bottle, until the cherry softens into leather and tobacco. Pour it with the roast lamb, or for anyone who wants a mellow red tonight.

glass.lead: Strawberry, red plum and dried cherry with leather and tobacco, often under the vanilla and coconut of American oak, at medium weight.

ladder.where: Rioja Alta and Rioja Alavesa, and Ribera del Duero's high plateau
Toro, Rioja Oriental, La Mancha and the Alentejo

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium to medium plus, tannin medium plus and firmer in Ribera and Toro, alcohol medium plus, body medium to full.

home.home: Spain, above all Rioja, where it leads a blend with Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo and the law sets its ageing as Crianza, Reserva or Gran Reserva. Ribera del Duero and Toro make it darker and firmer as Tinto Fino and Tinta de Toro, and La Mancha softer as Cencibel.
home.abroad: Across the border it is Tinta Roriz in the Douro, for Port and dry reds, and Aragonez in the Alentejo. Australia, southern Oregon and Texas tend to make it juicier, with ripe cherry and plum and softer tannin.

service.temp: 59 to 63 degrees Fahrenheit, 15 to 17 degrees Celsius, as for any medium red such as Rioja.
service.glass: A tall Bordeaux glass, with room to swirl, for Rioja and Ribera alike.
service.decant: Consider it for a young Ribera or Toro after a sample; decant an old Gran Reserva gently off its sediment.
service.age: Crianza within about five years; a Gran Reserva arrives already aged and can keep for decades more.

with.why: the classic match in Rioja and Ribera alike
smoky paprika meets the sweet vanilla of the cask
salt and nutty fat soften the grip
charred fat suits a dark, firm Ribera

labels.means: Rioja's ageing ladder for reds: at least two, three and five years, with one, one and two in barrel.
Tempranillo's names in Ribera del Duero, where it grows darker and firmer.
Tempranillo in Toro, dense and dark, and in La Mancha and Valdepeñas, softer and rounder.
Tempranillo in Portugal: Tinta Roriz in the Douro, Aragonez in the Alentejo and Lisboa.
A young red with no oak, or with a few months in barrel, below Crianza.

guest.q: What is the difference between a Crianza and a Gran Reserva?
guest.a: Time. A Crianza has aged at least two years, one in barrel. A Gran Reserva has aged at least five, two in barrel and two in bottle, so it is mellower, with tobacco, leather and dried cherry.

guest.q: Why does this Rioja smell of coconut and dill?
guest.a: That is American oak, the traditional cask of Rioja's older houses. The grape gives the strawberry and cherry; the barrel gives the vanilla, coconut and dill.

guest.q: Is a Ribera del Duero the same grape as a Rioja?
guest.a: Yes, Tempranillo, called Tinto Fino there. Hot days and cold nights on the high plateau give thicker skins, so Ribera tends to be darker and firmer, with blackberry where Rioja has strawberry.

compare.tell: Sangiovese is tarter, with sour cherry, tomato leaf and dried oregano; Tempranillo is softer in acidity, with strawberry and, in Rioja, the dill and coconut of American oak.
Grenache is paler, softer in tannin and warmer in alcohol, with raspberry, kirsch and white pepper; Tempranillo is deeper and firmer, with tobacco and the vanilla of the cask.
Graciano, its partner in the Rioja blend, is deeper in colour and sharper in acidity, with violet and a peppery lift; Tempranillo is rounder, with strawberry and leather.

cards.front: Tempranillo goes by other names. Which in Ribera, Toro, La Mancha and Portugal?
cards.back: Tinto Fino or Tinta del País in Ribera del Duero, Tinta de Toro in Toro, Cencibel in La Mancha, Tinta Roriz in the Douro and Aragonez in the Alentejo.

cards.front: Tempranillo as red Rioja: the minimum ageing of Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva?
cards.back: Crianza two years, one in barrel. Reserva three, one in barrel and six months in bottle. Gran Reserva five, two in barrel and two in bottle.

cards.front: Tempranillo: what does its name mean, and who are its parents?
cards.back: Temprano is Spanish for early: it ripens weeks before Garnacha. DNA work published in 2012 found its parents to be Albillo Mayor, a white grape, and Benedicto, a grape now almost lost.

questions.q: A red poured blind is garnet at the rim, with dried cherry, strawberry, leather and tobacco under a sweet layer of coconut and dill, medium acidity and medium plus tannin. Which grape and place fit?
questions.exp: Dill and coconut point to American oak, the traditional cask of Rioja, over Tempranillo's dried cherry and leather. Chianti Classico, the nearest miss, would be tarter, with tomato leaf and higher acidity.

questions.q: A guest who loves Rioja asks for the same grape on the Portuguese page of the list. Which names do you look for on the Douro and Alentejo reds?
questions.exp: Tempranillo is Tinta Roriz in the Douro and Aragonez in the Alentejo. Touriga Nacional and Jaen, the nearest miss, are two other grapes: Jaen is Mencía.

questions.q: A guest asks why the Ribera del Duero tastes darker and firmer than the Rioja beside it, though both are Tempranillo. What is the main reason?
opts: Hot days and cold nights thicken the skins
The law makes it blend with Garnacha
The law makes it age far longer
It is fermented with whole bunches
questions.exp: On Ribera's high plateau, hot days and cold nights give a thicker skinned grape with deeper colour and firmer tannin. Its legal ageing minimums match Rioja's barrel time, so longer ageing is the nearest wrong answer.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it; nothing contradicts TASTE.world old. Portugal sits in abroad as across the border, though both Iberian countries are the Old World home the plan names.

The ageing ladder (Crianza 24 months with 12 in barrel, Reserva 36 with 12 in barrel and 6 in bottle, Gran Reserva 60 with 24 and 24), American oak and its coconut, vanilla and dill, the names Tinto Fino, Tinta del País, Tinta de Toro, Cencibel, Tinta Roriz and Aragonez, Ribera's thicker skins from hot days and cold nights, and lamb, chorizo and Manchego all stand on the Codex's own Rioja, Ribera del Duero, Rueda and Toro, La Mancha, Douro, Lisboa and Alentejo records and on GRID_READS.

Parentage (Albillo Mayor and Benedicto, published in 2012) stands on the University of La Rioja's own research record of the paper; the name from temprano, early, on the Oxford Companion and on the Codex's own Régionale question i-8lrwa2oc. Texas stands on the Texas A&M AgriLife variety list; southern Oregon and McLaren Vale on the Codex's Oregon and McLaren Vale records. Argentina, named in the plan's modeWhy, is left out for want of a second source.
This session reached search alone; no host could be fetched, so each address is cited as the search results gave it and a checker should open them.

The Codex's Régionale question i-8lrwa2oc calls Tempranillo the most widely planted red in Spain, a volatile ranking the house rules keep out of new prose; the Douro record's the most planted for Touriga Franca is the same kind. GRAPES gives Tempranillo's tannin as medium plus to high and the grid medium to medium plus; the structure line takes medium plus and firmer in Ribera and Toro, which both allow.

checked.verdict: Sound after three fixes. The Rioja and Ribera rules, the Iberian names, the parentage and the American oak all stand; the sale put a Reserva's whole three years in barrel and bottle, abroad leaned on fruit led, and the close shared its construction with another grape's name story.
changed: lines.s45: The close used the construction the name comes from, which Sauvignon Blanc's close shares, among a dozen closes on a name. It now opens on the Spanish word itself and says what the grape does to earn it, and the line is 110 words where the first round's edit had left 113.

lines.sale: A Reserva was said to spend years in barrel and bottle, which reads as its whole time in wood and glass. The rule is 36 months at least with 12 in barrel and 6 in bottle, the rest where the cellar chooses, so the sale now says part in barrel and part in bottle.
worlds.home.abroad: Fruit led named no fruit, a family word in disguise. Ripe cherry and plum, which the entry's own warm rung allows, take its place, and tend to keeps the hedge.
open: Abroad's juicier, softer style for Australia, southern Oregon and Texas is a fair hedge from the Codex's records and the author's sources, not a sourced tasting contrast.
GRAPES gives tannin medium plus to high and the grid medium to medium plus; the structure line's medium plus, firmer in Ribera and Toro, sits inside both.
